newsitem.title: UK: ATHLETICS-KIPKETER A MAN WITH A MISSION.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-KIPKETER A MAN WITH A MISSION.

text.p: Twenty-one years ago, long-striding Cuban Alberto Juantorena set a world record in the Olympic 800 metres final.
Juantorena, now a member of the International Amateur Athletic Federation (IAAF) council, was the last person to break the world record at a global championship.
Next week he will be a spectator as Wilson Kipketer, the Kenyan-born Dane, sets out on a mission which may give him sole possession of the oldest championship record and a bonus of $100,000.
Kipketer, the defending champion, has lived in Denmark since 1990 and was allowed to compete at the 1995 world championships in Gothenburg.
He ran away with the 800 title but was not allowed to compete in last year's Atlanta Olympics after objections from the Kenyan federation, who said he should be running for his native country.
This year, denied the chance of Olympic glory, the 26-year-old has been a man with a mission.
At the world indoor championships in March, Kipketer showed he does not need the apparently obligatory pacemaker to set world records, breaking the world mark in both the heats and the final.
On July 7 in Stockholm, he improved his best time by a tenth of a second to equal Seb Coe's 16-year-old world record of one minute 41.73 seconds.
Coe is an admirer of Kipketer after watching him for the first time at the Gothenburg world championships.
"He was the first person I had seen since Paul Ereng (Kenya's 1988 Olympic gold medallist) who I thought could break my record," Coe said.
Despite comfortably winning the gold medal, Kipketer maintained at the time that Coe's mark was out of his reach.
"That attitude may be part of the answer as to why the record has lasted so long," Coe responded. "You have to believe you can do it."
Under his new Polish coach Slavomir Novak, installed at the beginning of 1996, Kipketer seems to have gained in confidence.
But neither he, or his coach, will make predictions.
"All I do is get ready every year and do my best," Kipketer said.
Even after his Stockholm triumph, Kikpketer refused to get carried away. "I don't feel lucky about what I have done, only satisfied," he remarked.
Kipketer has also refused to divulge the secret of the training routine which has brought him two world indoor records and a share of the outdoor mark.
"I can't talk about my training," he said. "It's a secret and if I spoke about it, it would not be a secret anymore."
His joy in Stockholm when the time was confirmed was unconfined as he hugged his Danish fiancee Penilla. Next week he may have even more reason to celebrate.
